questions.prompt: (Exam 2021) From the text: "Today is the last day of school. We have a party with Mrs Blair, our English teacher." What are the pupils ready for?

options.text: a party
an English lesson
a school trip
an exam

questions.explanation: The pupils say "We have a party": the last day of school is a party day. The English lesson is only the subject of the teacher, named in the same sentence, and the text speaks of neither a school trip nor an exam.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2021) From the text: "Adam brings a chocolate cake. Tina, the Italian girl in our class, prepares drinks." Which sentence about the party is true?

options.text: Adam prepares the drinks and Tina brings a chocolate cake.
Adam brings a chocolate cake and Tina prepares drinks.
Adam and Tina both bring a chocolate cake.
Adam brings a birthday cake and Tina prepares sandwiches.

questions.explanation: Adam brings the chocolate cake, and Tina, the Italian girl, prepares the drinks. The first sentence gives each pupil the job of the other, the third one gives the cake to both, and a birthday cake and sandwiches are what a party often has, but the text names neither.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2021) True or false? The text says: "The girls are wearing pink skirts, yellow shirts and black shoes." and "Tina, the Italian girl in our class, prepares drinks." Statement: "Tina is wearing a pink skirt and a yellow shirt." Which answer does the text prove?

options.text: False: the pink skirts and the yellow shirts are the clothes of the boys of the class.
True: Tina is Italian, and Italian girls wear pink skirts.
True: Tina is a girl, and the girls wear pink skirts and yellow shirts.
False: Tina prepares the drinks, so she does not wear the party clothes.

questions.explanation: The text says that the girls wear pink skirts and yellow shirts, and Tina is one of the girls of the class, so the statement is true. The boys wear blue trousers and white shirts, nothing in the text links Italian girls to a colour, and preparing the drinks does not change what a girl wears.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2021) From the text: "Mr John, our Maths teacher, comes and says: 'Sorry, Mrs Blair is not coming today.'" Why does the Maths teacher come to the classroom?

options.text: To start a Maths lesson instead of the party.
To bring a present for all the pupils of the class.
To ask the pupils where Mrs Blair is today.
To tell the pupils that Mrs Blair is not coming.

questions.explanation: Mr John comes in to give a piece of news: the English teacher is not coming today. He does not start a lesson or bring a present, and he does not ask where she is, because he is the one who knows.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2021) True or false? The text says: "After an hour, Mrs Blair is not here yet." and then: "Sorry, Mrs Blair is not coming today." Statement: "Mrs Blair is coming late to the school party." Which answer does the text prove?

options.text: True: after an hour, Mrs Blair is not here yet, so she is late.
False: she is not coming at all today, as the Maths teacher says.
True: the party starts at 9 o'clock and she is not there at 9 o'clock.
False: she comes after the party is over.

questions.explanation: The pupils first think that Mrs Blair is late, but the Maths teacher then says that she is not coming today: she is absent, not late. The wait of one hour is only a detail that leads to the news, and nothing in the text says that she comes after the party.

questions.prompt: (Exam 2021) From the text: "It's 9 o'clock." and later: "After an hour, Mrs Blair is not here yet. What's happening? Is she absent?" At what time do the pupils begin to wonder where Mrs Blair is?

options.text: At 9 o'clock
At 10 o'clock
At 11 o'clock
At half past nine

questions.explanation: The text starts at 9 o'clock and says that one hour later Mrs Blair is still not there: 9 o'clock plus one hour is 10 o'clock. Nine o'clock is the time at which the party starts, and neither 11 o'clock nor half past nine is in the text.
